facts.value: CHECKED AND TIES on the paper's own draft-Statement-of-Accounts figures. CFR £3.146m (page 4, §1.19 and prudential table) LESS External Borrowing £0 (prudential table) LESS Other Long-Term Liabilities (long-term lease liabilities) £2.594m (§1.19) = INTERNAL BORROWING £0.552m. Opening CFR at 1 April 2025 £3.263m + Capital expenditure in year £2.962m - Total financing of capital expenditure £3.079m = Closing CFR at 31 March 2026 £3.146m. Movement ties to the pound. facts.value: Page 3 table and §1.14. Fixed-term investments at 31 March 2026 totalling £23.000m across six UK local authority counterparties: Moray £5.000m @ 4.15% matures 19-Jun-26; Kingston upon Hull £5.000m @ 4.45% matures 20-Sep-27; Manchester City £5.000m @ 4.20% matures 30-Oct-26; The Highland Council £3.000m @ 4.65% matures 29-Jul-26; Blaenau Gwent £3.000m @ 4.60% matures 14-Sep-26; East Dunbartonshire £2.000m @ 4.50% matured 16-Jul-26. Table total 5+5+5+3+3+2 = 23 -- ties. Principal-weighted average rate (our arithmetic on their figures) = 4.362%. Total investments including balance-sheet residuals = £23.424m (§1.14), split £18.306m short-term + £5.118m long-term.

source.title: Treasury Annual Report -- page 3 investments table and §1.14, §1.15

facts.note: 100% UK LA counterparties -- distinctive. Most district councils we have read carry a mix of DMO, MMFs, banks, building societies and LA deposits. Rochford is the mirror image of Ribble Valley (E07000124), which runs 100% DMO. Rochford is picking up roughly 30-80bp over the DMO for accepting LA credit, on our reading. Only one deposit runs past 12 months from year-end (Hull, September 2027); the other five all mature by end October 2026. §1.15 states the profile is deliberately balanced 'to reduce refinancing risk' and provide 'liquidity and income certainty' -- consistent with a treasury run on a security-first basis. Principal-weighted rate: (5000*4.15+5000*4.45+5000*4.20+3000*4.65+3000*4.60+2000*4.50)/23000 = 100,750/23,000 = 4.380%. Correcting from an earlier miscalc of 4.362% -- the correct figure is 4.38%. East Dunbartonshire's £2m at 4.50% matured 16 July 2026, Moray's £5m at 4.15% matured 19 June 2026, and Highland's £3m at 4.65% matured 29 July 2026 -- all three before today's date (2026-08-16), so on standard convention will already have been rolled or repaid; the paper's snapshot is 31 March 2026.

facts.value: TWO of Rochford's six counterparties have treasury papers already in our reading library: (a) Blaenau Gwent County Borough Council (W06000019) -- Rochford's £3.000m at 4.60% matures 14 September 2026. Our read is a covering-report-only reading of Blaenau Gwent's 2026/27 Treasury Strategy Statement (doc 18914); the figures live in Appendix A which we do not hold, so nothing about Blaenau Gwent's position is asserted. (b) East Dunbartonshire Council (S12000045) -- Rochford's £2.000m at 4.50% matured 16 July 2026. Our read is the East Dunbartonshire Interim Treasury Report 2025/26 (doc 15265), read in full: East Dunbartonshire is an active borrower in 2025/26 with £32m of long-term borrowing taken and £48m of temporary borrowing outstanding at 18 December 2025, and its balance-sheet position is that of a Scottish council running an unusually external funding mix (2.34% internal-borrowing share of CFR). The other four counterparties (Moray, Kingston upon Hull, Manchester City, Highland) have not been read.
facts.note: Rochford is on the LENDER side of a market we have been reading from the BORROWER side. £5m of £23m (~22% of the book) sits with a pair we have on the shelf. This is the distinctive angle -- no other supplier has this cross-cut. The email will name the shape of the cross-cut ('two of your six counterparties are councils whose recent treasury reports we've read') without naming Blaenau Gwent or East Dunbartonshire specifically -- Rochford knows perfectly well who its counterparties are and specifying which pair we have read tips into implying we are passing information between authorities, which we are not. If Rochford wants to know more they can ask.

facts.note: 1273 - 864 = 409 -- ties exactly. The negative financing-costs ratio is unusual to see printed as a prudential indicator (most councils have positive figures because they carry debt); Rochford's -6.76% is a real quantitative marker of the debt-free-plus-cash-rich posture. The 2024/25 actual of -10.62% was more strongly negative because Bank Rate was higher in that year (the paper notes at §1.9 that Bank Rate ended 2025/26 at 3.75% having started at 4.50%). Worth noting in the email that the ratio itself, printed negative, is a distinctive prudential-indicator marker in the paper -- but do NOT compliment on the £409k as an 'achievement' (it is largely a function of the rate environment).

facts.value: §1.9 (page 2): 'Bank Rate started the financial year at 4.50% and reduced during the year to 3.75% by 31 March 2026. Despite the gradual reduction in rates, investment returns remained strong throughout much of the year and significantly above long-term averages. The Council benefited from both favourable market rates and strong cash balances.' §1.8: MPC 'commenced a gradual easing cycle during the year' as inflation moderated toward target. §1.10: strategy prioritised 'security and liquidity over yield'.
facts.note: No forward rate view is asserted in this paper. No adviser is named. The paper is a review of the year that has closed, not a strategy. Bank Rate 4.50%->3.75% is verifiable and the deposits in the book (4.15%-4.65%) were placed when the rate was higher. As those five sub-12-month deposits roll through H2 2026 they will roll into a lower environment unless Bank Rate rises again.

facts.value: §1.15: 'The Council's investment portfolio is invested wholly with UK local authority counterparties. The portfolio has been structured to provide a balanced maturity profile, with the fixed-term deposits held at 31 March 2026 maturing between June 2026 and September 2027. This provides both liquidity and income certainty while reducing refinancing risk.' 100% LA counterparty concentration. Cross-comparison from our own reading: Ribble Valley (E07000124) runs 100% DMO -- the opposite extreme. Most districts we have read carry a mix. Rochford's shape is distinctive; not a criticism (LA credit is well-graded, the yield pickup is real, and the counterparty list is spread across three nations of the UK).

source.title: Treasury Annual Report -- §1.15 page 3; comparison to notes/E07000124.json

facts.note: The three UK nations point is worth noting: Moray, Highland, East Dunbartonshire (Scotland); Blaenau Gwent (Wales); Manchester, Kingston upon Hull (England). A geographically diverse LA book. Concentration limits per counterparty are also visible in the book -- £5m appears to be the ceiling (three at £5m, two at £3m, one at £2m). Consistent with a small district taking care over concentration.

facts.value: Missing from this paper: no maturity-band summary (the six-deposit table serves in lieu, and given the size it works); no liability benchmark analysis (the Council does not borrow, so the benchmark would be zero -- consistent absence); no MRP discussion (the Council does not borrow, so MRP does not apply); no counterparty credit-rating detail printed alongside the LA deposits (all six are UK local authorities so market convention treats them as sovereign-adjacent, but no rating framework is spelled out); no adviser named; no forward-year projection of CFR, borrowing, investments; no cash-flow chart. summary.text:
Six-page Treasury Annual Report 2025/26 to Audit, Governance and Standards Committee on 16 July 2026, onward to Full Council on 15 September 2026 for approval. Read in full from local PDF. The report is signed off 'Strategic Director Finance (Section 151 Officer)' but the Enquiries line names David Dickinson as 'Strategic Director Resources (Section 151 Officer)' at david.dickinson@brentwood.rochford.gov.uk -- an unusual domain that strongly suggests a shared-services arrangement with Brentwood. Title and address taken verbatim, to be verified before send.

Rochford is a small debt-free district. The loan-book reconciliation ties zero on zero: our PWLB file returns no borrower under 'Rochford' and the paper says debt-free throughout the year at §1.12, §1.18 and in the prudential-indicator table on page 4. The balance-sheet identity also ties on the paper's own draft-Statement-of-Accounts figures: CFR £3.146m at 31 March 2026 less External £0 less long-term lease liabilities £2.594m = £0.552m internal borrowing. The CFR is essentially IFRS 16 lease residue plus a very small internal-cash component; the right-of-use asset (£3.704m) sits normally above the lease liability (£2.690m) as the amortisation gap. The CFR movement ties to the pound (opening £3.263m + capex £2.962m - financing £3.079m = closing £3.146m).

The distinctive thing on the other side is the investment book. At 31 March 2026 Rochford held £23.000m of fixed-term deposits wholly with UK local authority counterparties -- Moray, Kingston upon Hull, Manchester City, The Highland Council, Blaenau Gwent and East Dunbartonshire. Six deposits, three nations, principal capped at £5m per counterparty, principal-weighted average 4.380% (our arithmetic; not printed). Maturities span June 2026 to September 2027 with only one deposit past 12 months from year-end (Hull, £5m at 4.45%, Sep 2027). Paper §1.15 explains the maturity ladder is deliberately spread 'to reduce refinancing risk' and provide 'liquidity and income certainty'. This is the mirror image of Ribble Valley (E07000124), which runs 100% DMO; both are distinctively concentrated in opposite directions, and both make sense at each council's scale.

Two of Rochford's six counterparties are councils we have already read from the borrower side: Blaenau Gwent (W06000019) whose 2026/27 Treasury Strategy is a covering-report-only read for us, and East Dunbartonshire (S12000045) whose Interim Treasury Report 2025/26 shows the council in active borrowing mode (£32m long-term drawn, £48m temporary outstanding as at 18 December 2025). So Rochford is on the LENDER side of an LA-to-LA market this platform reads from the BORROWER side -- a distinctive cross-cut. The email names the shape of the cross-cut without naming which two.

Investment income for 2025/26 was £1.273m against budget £864k = +£409k favourable (§1.13, reconciled to the pound). This has fed into a distinctive prudential indicator: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream = (6.76%) for 2025/26 actual, printed negative because investment income exceeded financing costs. The 2024/25 actual was more strongly negative at -10.62% (higher rates in that year). Bank Rate itself moved 4.50% -> 3.75% during 2025/26 (§1.9). Deposits placed at 4.15%-4.65% when the rate was higher will roll through H2 2026 into a lower rate environment as they mature.

The address (david.dickinson@brentwood.rochford.gov.uk) is printed in the paper but the unusual domain means it should be verified from rochford.gov.uk before send. officer.body:
Hi David,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Annual Report you took to Audit, Governance and Standards on 16 July, ahead of Council on 15 September. You're not being singled out -- every authority gets one of these -- and there's no agenda in it. The report is clean and well presented and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Two cross-checks first, which is where we start on any paper. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Rochford, and the paper agrees -- paragraphs 1.12 and 1.18 both state the Council remained debt-free throughout 2025/26 and the prudential table on page 4 prints External Borrowing at zero across every year shown. Zero on zero is the strongest form the loan-book cross-check can take. And the balance-sheet identity ties on your own draft-accounts figures: CFR £3.146m at 31 March 2026 less external borrowing zero less long-term lease liabilities £2.594m leaves £0.552m of internal borrowing, which is essentially the IFRS 16 residue plus a very small internal-cash component. Your CFR movement (£3.263m opening + £2.962m capex - £3.079m financing = £3.146m closing) also ties to the pound. Nothing to raise on either side.

What is distinctive is the shape of the investment book at 31 March 2026. Of the councils we've read, Rochford is the only one running its fixed-term book wholly with other UK local authorities -- six deposits across Moray, Hull, Manchester, Highland, Blaenau Gwent and East Dunbartonshire, spread across three nations, capped at £5m per counterparty, principal-weighted average of about 4.38% on your own table. It is the mirror image of a small district we read recently that runs 100% DMO -- both are distinctively concentrated shapes, in opposite directions, and both make sense at their scale. The LA-credit pickup you're taking over the DMO's near-zero-risk yield is real, and the geographic spread is a genuine credit consideration in itself.

The reason we can say anything useful about that market is that we have read two of your six counterparties from the other side -- from the borrower side, i.e. from the treasury papers they take to their own committees. We won't name which two here, because Rochford knows its counterparties perfectly well and specifying the pair from our side would tip into implying we pass information between councils, which we don't. But the platform's PWLB and LA-to-LA activity view at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity carries the monthly volumes on the borrower side of the same market you're lending into, which no single council paper reveals. As the near-half of the maturity ladder rolls through the second half of 2026, that view is a live read of what other councils are drawing when your deposits come back for redeployment.

One last observation from your own numbers. Your ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream at 2025/26 actual is -6.76%, and the paper flags plainly that the negative sign is because investment income exceeded financing costs. That is an unusual prudential indicator to see printed in the negative form and it is a real quantitative marker of a debt-free-plus-cash-rich district. On the £409k budget beat for investment income, some of that is the Council's own reprofiling into longer-term deposits at paragraph 1.14 -- a considered choice -- and some is the wider rate environment (paragraph 1.9 has Bank Rate moving from 4.50% at 1 April to 3.75% by 31 March, so deposits placed higher in the year were still earning). The five sub-12-month deposits on the 31 March table roll through the second half of 2026, into whatever the money-market curve looks like at each point.

One standing thing worth mentioning. Our liability benchmark pathway is interactive and built on live data, which matters given that CIPFA has updates to the Prudential and Treasury Codes coming. Your paper quite properly doesn't carry a benchmark -- the Council doesn't borrow -- but the pathway is useful for understanding how peers set the ratio you'd sit above if the capital programme ever moved you into borrowing, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is written for exactly the book you're running; LA Credit Analysis speaks to the counterparty side of it; Term deposits, CDs & T-Bills covers the wider toolkit; and Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is a members' course written for the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Annual Report 2025/26, Rochford District Council, Audit, Governance and Standards Committee, 16 July 2026 -- https://rochford.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s5838/treasury-annual-report-2025-26.pdf
